segment_name: Opening: The Utilitarian Machine and Its Discontents

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Dickens opens this novel basically as a vaudeville turn — that Gradgrind is fundamentally a comic grotesque. Can you read us that opening description, the 'square wall of a forehead,' the neckcloth, all of it — and make the case that this is comedy first and critique second?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the passage aloud and establish the performative, theatrical reading as the opening position — sets up immediate friction with both Edmund and Daniel

questions.question: Daniel, Oliver's just made Gradgrind funny. You've told me you think that's almost a dangerous reading — that the comedy lets us off the hook. What's at stake if we laugh too easily at Thomas Gradgrind, sir?
questions.intent: Provoke direct pushback on Oliver's theatrical reading; get Daniel to articulate the class machinery argument and the idea that the joke is part of how the ideology conceals itself

questions.question: Edmund, I want to bring you in on something specific — that neckcloth image, 'trained to take him by the throat with an unaccommodating grasp, like a stubborn fact.' Daniel says that's the architecture of power colonising Gradgrind's body. Oliver says it's a stage direction. You've called it something else entirely — moral portraiture of a man who's made a spiritual choice. Who's right?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to articulate the moral-spiritual reading against both the theatrical and the ideological, and expose the core three-way disagreement about what the physical description is actually doing

questions.question: Daniel, you've flagged something that I don't think the others have quite reckoned with — whose imagination are we actually mourning here? Because Dickens is writing this for a middle-class audience, and the children in that schoolroom are poor. Is there something uncomfortable about the way the novel asks us to grieve for Fancy on behalf of people we'll never meet?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's class critique of the Fancy argument itself — push toward the sharpest version of his reading and see if Edmund or Oliver will defend Dickens against it

questions.question: Edmund, last one — you've described the M'Choakumchild passage as a Christian meditation, practically a question about grace. Daniel thinks it's a prosecution of a system. Oliver thinks it's operatic theatre. Can you read us the Morgiana line — 'dost thou think that thou wilt always kill outright the robber Fancy' — and tell us why you think Dickens is asking a question about the soul rather than about schools?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the most charged reading of the passage, let Edmund go full moral-spiritual, and give Daniel and Oliver the chance to respond — end on disagreement rather than resolution

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that the questions are designed to surface progressively. Start with Oliver's theatrical reading because it's the most accessible and enjoyable — get the room warm before Daniel's class critique sharpens things. The key cross-engagement is between Edmund and Daniel: Edmund sees a man who chose spiritual bankruptcy, Daniel sees a man produced by a system. Don't let that disagreement get abstract — keep pulling it back to specific words in the text. Oliver is the wild card who can destabilise both: he'll find Gradgrind funny when Edmund wants solemnity and find him entertaining when Daniel wants outrage. Use Oliver to keep the energy up and stop either of the other two from getting too settled. Avoid letting anyone give a lecture — if someone starts listing points, interrupt and ask them to read the passage instead.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund says the problem is a human choice to submit to calculation; Daniel says there is no choice — the system produces the subject. This is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be named directly when both have spoken.

Oliver's claim that the comedy has to work or the critique collapses cuts against Daniel's worry that the comedy lets us off the hook — these are almost mirror-image arguments about the same formal feature.
All three want to quote the neckcloth line but for completely different reasons — this is the ideal moment to put all three readings side by side and ask the listeners which one they believe.

Daniel's question about whose imagination is being protected (the poor get neither facts nor feeling) has no direct answer from Edmund or Oliver in pre-interview — this should be left open and unresolved, it's the most uncomfortable idea in the segment.

segment_name: Louisa's Hollow Heart: How Fact Crushes Feeling

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our pre-chat that really stuck with me — that Louisa isn't just a victim of bad parenting, she's a *product* of a system that's working exactly as intended. Walk us through that passage — 'How could you give me life, and take from me all the inappreciable things that raise it from the state of conscious death?' — because on the surface that sounds like a daughter having a breakdown. But you're hearing something colder in it, aren't you?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to make the structural/class argument upfront and provocatively — sets up the disagreement with Edmund immediately

questions.question: Edmund, I can already see you wanting to jump in there. Because when you read that same scene — Louisa collapsing before her father — you called it a *spiritual* crisis, not a political one. Dickens gives her this language of angels and demons — 'I have almost repulsed and crushed my better angel into a demon' — and you said that's not metaphor, that's theology. So who's right? Is Gradgrind a class enforcer or a soul-murderer? Can he be both?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to articulate the moral-spiritual reading in direct contrast to Rosen's materialist one — get the core disagreement on the table

questions.question: Oliver, you've been listening to Daniel say this is structural dispossession and Edmund say it's spiritual desolation, and I suspect you think they're both missing something. Because you kept coming back to *performance* in our chat — you said read these lines aloud and you hear a Jacobean actress, not a Victorian case study. So is Dickens actually doing something different from what either of them is describing? Is Louisa giving a speech, not a confession?
questions.intent: Introduce the theatrical reading as a provocation to both — gets Trevelyan's strongest take while implicitly challenging the seriousness of both Edmund and Daniel's framings

questions.question: But here's what I want to push on, Daniel — because Oliver just pointed to that image in the early chapters, 'a starved imagination keeping life in itself somehow.' All three of you quoted that line to me separately, which tells me it's doing something important. And you read it as evidence of *resistance* — there's still a flicker the system hasn't killed. But by the end of the novel, what actually happens to that flicker? Does Louisa recover? Or does Dickens just... leave her there?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to confront the novel's bleak ending and whether his 'resistance' reading can survive it — also invites Edmund and Oliver to contest his answer

questions.question: Edmund, last one for this segment — and it's a bit of a challenge. Daniel argued earlier that Louisa's eloquence in that confrontation scene is actually a form of submission — she's explaining her own brokenness to the man who broke her, not demanding anything back. And Oliver might say the theatrical extravagance of her language is Dickens the entertainer at work. So my question is: does Louisa's self-awareness save her, in your reading? Or is the ability to name what was stolen from you a very different thing from getting it back?
questions.intent: Close the segment on the hardest question — whether insight equals recovery — and give Edmund the chance to either defend or modify his moral-redemption reading under pressure from both other experts

steering_notes: Let the Rosen-Edmund disagreement run hot early — they're talking about the same passages from almost incompatible frameworks (class structure vs. spiritual anthropology) and that friction is the engine of the segment. Trevelyan is the wild card who can puncture both when they get too earnest — use him to reset energy when the debate gets too abstract. Watch for the moment when all three are quoting the same line (c3:p19, c21:p128) and make that explicit on air: 'You've all reached for the same passage and read something completely different in it' — that's a great radio moment. The segment should end on the unresolved question of whether Louisa actually recovers, because Dickens himself seems to refuse the comfort of an answer.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen says Louisa's eloquence is 'internalized domination' — Edmund will almost certainly read the same eloquence as her humanity persisting; name this contradiction directly and let them go at it

Both Rosen and Trevelyan quote 'a starved imagination keeping life in itself somehow' (c3:p19) but to opposite ends — Rosen sees residual resistance, Trevelyan sees Dickens finding grotesque comedy in survival. Get them to argue about what that 'somehow' is actually doing.

Edmund's claim that the demon-and-angel language is theological (echoing Milton) vs. Trevelyan's claim that it's theatrical performance writing — these aren't mutually exclusive but they feel opposed, and both experts will dig in

Rosen's prediction that Dickens offers no redemption for Louisa vs. Edmund's implied arc toward moral and spiritual recovery — this is the clearest factual disagreement about the novel and should be named explicitly

segment_name: The Loom and the Law: Stephen Blackpool's Impossible Choice

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these law passages are incantations, not arguments — that Dickens is trying to break us open rather than convince us of anything. Can you read us that Rachael line, 'Can a man have no soul of his own,' and show us what you mean? What does hearing it actually do that reading it on the page doesn't?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the passage aloud and make the case for the theatrical-voice reading, which sets up Daniel's structural rebuttal and Edmund's existential one

questions.question: Daniel, you heard Oliver frame that as a piece of rhetorical performance. But your read is almost the opposite — you've said Stephen's virtue is *irrelevant* to a system that grinds him anyway. So when Rachael asks 'can a man have no soul of his own,' is she asking a philosophical question, or is she just describing the machinery?
questions.intent: Force the philosophical-vs-structural fault line into the open — Edmund will want to defend the philosophical reading, Oliver the performative one

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Stephen a study in a good man made powerless, and you've said he can only be redeemed by sacrifice and faith. Daniel's going to tell me that's exactly the reading that makes us miss the radicalism. Convince me you're not just letting Dickens off the hook by turning a structural argument into a martyrdom story.
questions.intent: Direct provocation designed to get Edmund to articulate his sharpest take while inviting Daniel's explicit pushback — the real disagreement in this panel

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to the dead sister — 'young and misshapen, awlung o' sickly air as had'n no need to be.' You've called this preventable murder. Edmund thinks Dickens frames it through love and memory, not a reform programme. Oliver says that phrase 'had'n no need to be' is where the performance goes quiet. Who's right about what Dickens is actually doing there?
questions.intent: Triangulate the three readings around a single passage — forces all three experts to commit to an interpretation of the same lines

questions.question: Last one, and I'll throw this to Oliver first but I want everyone in. Stephen walks out of Bounderby's office having convinced nobody in power of anything. Oliver, you say he convinces *us* through musicality and moral clarity. But does Dickens actually believe that's enough? Is the novel saying the voice matters, or is it saying even the most devastating voice gets swallowed by the machine?
questions.intent: Close the segment on the deepest tension — does art change anything, does sympathy change anything — and give all three a chance to land their final position

steering_notes: The real engine of this segment is the Daniel-vs-Edmund fault line: structural critique versus moral tragedy. Oliver is the wild card who can destabilize both by insisting the whole thing is a performance problem, not an ideology problem. Let Daniel and Edmund clash directly on the martyrdom question — that's the moment the segment catches fire. Don't let Oliver stay safely in the 'voice and rhythm' lane the whole time; push him to say whether Dickens thinks the voice actually *works* as a political instrument. Keep the passage readings in — especially the Rachael question and the dead sister lines — because the text will do more work than any of the experts' glosses.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver reads 'Can a man have no soul of his own' aloud, then Daniel immediately reframes it as structural description rather than existential question — direct collision of theatrical and Marxist readings

Edmund's claim that Stephen 'can only be redeemed by sacrifice and faith' is the precise sentence Daniel flagged in pre-interview as the reading that neutralizes the novel's radicalism — surface this explicitly

Daniel and Edmund both want to quote 'show me the law to help me' but for opposite reasons: Daniel as proof the law is a tool of class management, Edmund as proof of Stephen's spiritual desolation — let them argue over the same line

Oliver's insistence that Stephen has genuine rhetorical agency through dialect sits in productive tension with Daniel's claim that Stephen's virtue is irrelevant to the system — worth surfacing mid-segment

segment_name: Dickens Performing Gradgrind: Wit, Satire, and the Comic Collapse of Reason

questions.question: Oliver, you've said this book has to be *heard* to be understood — that the satire is really a performance. So let's test that. Take the sponge passage — c13:p0 — 'wipe out all their tears with one dirty little bit of sponge.' Why does that land differently when you say it out loud? What is Dickens actually *doing* with that detail?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform or at least enact his thesis — that these passages collapse into absurdity through sound, not just meaning — and draw out his strongest claim that the comedy has teeth, not just warmth

questions.question: Edmund, you've pushed back on the idea that Gradgrind is a symbol of anything — capitalism, utilitarianism, whatever. You say he's just a *man*, a specific self-deceived man in a ridiculous room. But Daniel is going to tell you that Observatory isn't ridiculous — it's actually a perfect machine for making real people disappear. Who's right? Is Gradgrind a comic portrait of one fool, or is the fool doing something systemically useful?
questions.intent: Set up the central disagreement between Edmund's moral-individual reading and Daniel's structural reading — force Edmund to defend the line between 'portrait of a man' and 'indictment of a system'

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat that really stuck with me — that we're laughing at Gradgrind's rusty compasses when we should be *horrified* at what he's measuring. But here's my question: does Dickens know that? Is he in on the joke, or is he — as you put it — funnier about Gradgrind than he realises?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's sharpest and most provocative claim — that Dickens's comedy unwittingly serves as cover for what the novel is actually documenting — and see if Oliver and Edmund will defend Dickens against the suggestion he's complicit

questions.question: Edmund, let's talk about c22:p19 — 'to do him justice he had.' You've said that phrase is crucial, that Dickens is holding moral judgment and human sympathy in suspension. But Oliver thinks the comedy has teeth, and Daniel thinks Gradgrind becomes an MP and nothing changes. Does giving Gradgrind his 'justice' let him — and us — off the hook?
questions.intent: Probe the tension between Edmund's sympathetic reading of Gradgrind's sincerity and both Oliver's insistence that the comedy doesn't excuse and Daniel's structural argument that individual moral redemption is beside the point

questions.question: Last one — and I want all three of you on this. Oliver, you called the Parliament passage a music hall turn, a *bit*. If Dickens is doing a bit, if this is essentially performance and entertainment, does that blunt the political edge — or is that exactly how the attack lands? Can something be a great joke *and* a serious indictment at the same time, or does the laughter let everyone off too easy?
questions.intent: Force a final synthesis or showdown on the core question of the segment — whether comedy is the vehicle for critique or its escape valve — designed to get all three experts talking over each other in the best possible way

steering_notes: The productive fault line here is not really Oliver vs Edmund — they actually agree Dickens is a comic artist, not a pamphleteer — but both of them vs Daniel, who wants to flip the comedy inside out and show the horror underneath the joke. Let that tension breathe. Don't rush to resolve it. If Oliver and Edmund start agreeing too readily, push them toward Daniel's reading of c3:p11: ask whether Louisa's desire for beauty is heartwarming or whether it's already doomed and contained before she even stands up from the fence. The sponge passage (c13:p0) is the flashpoint — all three want to quote it and for completely different reasons. Get them to argue about the *same sentence* and you'll have the segment.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund says the Observatory is a portrait of 'a ridiculous man in a ridiculous room' — Daniel says it's 'a perfect machine for making human suffering administratively invisible.' Same passage, opposite conclusions. Put that directly to both of them.

Oliver argues the comedy has teeth and we laugh at Gradgrind so we don't excuse him — Daniel argues the laughter is exactly what excuses him, because we're inside the joke too. That's a direct and productive contradiction worth surfacing explicitly.

Edmund's reading of 'to do him justice he had' (c22:p19) as moral realism and human sympathy collides with Daniel's point that Gradgrind becomes MP anyway — ask Edmund whether the novel's sympathy for Gradgrind is something Dickens earns or something that lets the system off the hook.
All three want to quote the sponge passage for different reasons — this is the single best moment to force direct cross-engagement. Ask each in turn: same words, what are you hearing?

segment_name: The Smoke-Filled Streets: Coketown as Character

questions.question: Oliver, I want to start with you because you used a word in our chat that stuck with me — you said Dickens is 'seduced' by these machines even as he's horrifying us with them. Can you read that opening of c9:p0 — the fairy palaces, the serpents, the mad elephants — and then tell me: is Dickens actually enjoying himself here? Because it almost sounds like he is.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read the c9:p0 passage aloud and open his 'fascination vs. horror' tension, which directly sets up Rosen's structural critique and Leigh's moral reading as competing responses

questions.question: Daniel, I can see you itching to jump in there. Because I think you'd say Oliver's framing — Dickens the baroque entertainer, seduced by the machinery — is actually missing what makes this dangerous. That ledger passage in c12:p0, 'so much fuel consumed, so many powers worn out, so much money made' — you read that very differently, don't you? Can you do what you described to me: read it like a cold accountant, and tell us what we're actually hearing?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to perform the c12:p0 passage as a ledger reading, then articulate his structural capitalism argument — directly challenging Trevelyan's aesthetic framing and setting up the Leigh vs. Rosen disagreement about sympathy vs. system

questions.question: Edmund, here's where I want to push you, because you told me these passages are fundamentally about *character* — not policy, not aesthetics. And you flagged that line in c8:p1 about Providence making workers 'only hands' as something you wanted to get to. So: when Dickens puts Stephen Blackpool on the page with that savage irony sitting over him — does that make Stephen a victim of a system, like Daniel's saying, or does it set up a question about whether a *good man* can survive that system? Because those feel like very different novels to me.
questions.intent: Force the Leigh vs. Rosen disagreement into the open: moral survival of the individual versus systemic dehumanization. Get Leigh to quote c8:p1 and stake out his virtue-and-will position explicitly

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund is basically saying the novel asks whether goodness can survive Coketown — that it's a tragedy of individual character. And I think you'd say that framing is itself part of the problem? That asking 'can Stephen stay good?' is exactly the kind of sympathy that lets the system off the hook?
questions.intent: Sharpen the central disagreement: Leigh's humanist moralism versus Rosen's structural critique. Make Rosen articulate why sympathy is the wrong response — and let Leigh respond to that provocation directly

questions.question: Oliver, you've been listening to these two argue about whether Dickens is a moralist or a systems analyst — but I want to drag you back to something. You said in our conversation that the *music* of this novel is where the real argument lives, that the politics follow from the language rather than the other way round. Does either of their readings actually account for why these passages *work* on the page? Or are they both explaining away the thing Dickens is actually doing?
questions.intent: Give Trevelyan the last destabilizing move — his aesthetic argument as a challenge to both Leigh and Rosen simultaneously — and create a three-way moment where everyone has to defend their framework

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that should be exploited rather than resolved: Trevelyan on language and performance, Rosen on structural capitalism, Leigh on moral character. Don't let any one framing 'win' — keep pushing back with the others' positions. The key cross-engagement is Leigh vs. Rosen on whether sympathy for Stephen Blackpool is a humanist strength or an ideological distraction. Save that fight for the middle. Trevelyan should open and close — his aesthetic frame is the most accessible entry point and the best destabilizing exit. Push everyone to read aloud where possible: c9:p0, c12:p0, and c8:p1 all reward performance.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan says Dickens is 'seduced' by industrial scale — Rosen would argue that seduction IS the ideological operation of capital, which makes it worse not better; these need to collide

Rosen says sympathy isn't the point, lucidity is — Leigh built his entire pre-interview argument around individual moral fibre and the question of Stephen's virtue; put those two statements back-to-back and let them fight

Leigh and Trevelyan actually agree that formal beauty is morally serious, not decorative — but for completely different reasons (Leigh: beauty IS the moral argument; Trevelyan: beauty IS the argument, full stop). Surface this apparent agreement and then show the crack underneath it
The c12:p0 passage is wanted by all three experts — make sure each reads or responds to it, because they will perform it completely differently and that contrast is radio gold

segment_name: Breaking the Frame: Narrative Technique and the Reader's Awakening

questions.question: Oliver, you've said the novel's real argument is being made in the *voice* — that the baroque fury of Dickens's prose is itself the cure for Gradgrindery. Can you take us into that passage in c19:p95 — the 'Utilitarian economists, skeletons of schoolmasters' line — and show us what you mean? Because on the page it just looks like a rant. Why is it more than that?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform his reading aloud and make the case for voice-as-argument before Edmund and Daniel can frame the same passage politically or morally

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Gradgrind's moment of reckoning in c22:p18 a triumph of individual conscience — you're reading this almost as a theological drama, a man recovering his soul. But I want to push you: when Dickens writes 'making his facts and figures subservient to Faith, Hope, and Charity' in c26:p71, is that a genuinely hopeful ending, or is Dickens letting Gradgrind — and us — off the hook a little too easily?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's conservative-humanist reading while setting up Daniel's direct challenge about structural critique versus individual redemption

questions.question: Daniel, you've described Gradgrind's redemption as a trap — a piece of sentimentalism that lets readers feel catharsis while the machinery keeps running. But here's what I want to know: is that Dickens *failing*, or is it Dickens *knowing* something? Because he also has the narrator threaten the Utilitarians directly — 'in the day of your triumph...Reality will take a wolfish turn, and make an end of you.' That's not soft. Is Dickens playing both games at once?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to distinguish between Dickens's conscious radicalism and his ideological limits — and provoke Oliver and Edmund to defend their readings against the structural critique

questions.question: Let's get specific about c26:p14 — 'Everything was to be paid for. Nobody was ever on any account to give anybody anything.' All three of you want to quote this passage, which is interesting in itself. Daniel, you read the abolition of gratitude as a class weapon — it erases obligation between the powerful and the poor. Edmund, you read it as spiritual murder. Oliver, you've called it vaudeville. Can one passage really hold all three of those readings — or is someone wrong?
questions.intent: Force a direct three-way collision on the same passage to expose where the interpretive disagreements are genuinely irreconcilable

questions.question: Last one — and I want to end on this because it feels like the real fault line. Oliver, you've said meaning in this novel happens in the performance, in the voice. Daniel says the voice is almost a distraction — the catharsis it produces actually conceals the structural argument Dickens is making. Is it possible they're *both* right? Is the seductiveness of Dickens's prose style part of the problem the novel is diagnosing?
questions.intent: Create a synthesis moment that turns the conversation meta — asking whether Dickens's own narrative technique is complicit in the ideological softening Daniel identifies, and whether Oliver's reading of form can survive that challenge

steering_notes: The energy in this segment should feel like a genuine argument breaking out, not a seminar. The key fault line is between Oliver's formalist reading (voice and rhythm as argument), Edmund's moral-humanist reading (individual soul and conscience), and Daniel's structural critique (the system doesn't care about Gradgrind's feelings). Let them collide on c26:p14 specifically — all three want to quote it, which is a gift. Push toward the meta-question at the end: is Dickens's own seductive prose style part of what his novel is warning against? That's the live wire. Keep it pub-argumentative: interrupt, ask for quotes to be read aloud, make them defend their positions under pressure.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund reads Gradgrind's redemption in c22:p18 and c26:p71 as genuine moral awakening — Daniel reads it as structural evasion. This is the sharpest disagreement and should be surfaced early and returned to.

Oliver's claim that the hammering repetition in c26:p14 is 'almost slapstick' is a direct provocation to Edmund, who reads the same passage as articulating 'genuine moral horror' — get Edmund to respond to the comedic reading explicitly.

Daniel's point that the narrator *threatens* violence in c19:p95 ('Reality will take a wolfish turn') sits in tension with Edmund's Burke-ian reading of the same passage as classical moral appeal — they are reading the narrator's rhetorical *mode* completely differently.

Oliver's argument that prose excess is survival and cure needs to be tested against Daniel's claim that the same excess produces catharsis that obscures structural critique — this is a productive tension that could yield the segment's best moment.

segment_name: From Facts to Feeling: What Hard Times Demands of Us

questions.question: Oliver, you've said the Gradgrind transformation passage *has* to be read aloud — that the rhythm *is* the meaning. Would you do that for us now, c25:p74, 'Aged and bent he looked'? And then tell us: what does reading it out loud show you that silent reading misses?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform the passage, warm up the segment with voice and energy, and establish the aesthetic register before Rosen and Leigh complicate it

questions.question: Daniel, you heard Oliver read that. Beautiful, right? But you want to ask — wiser about *what*, exactly? Gradgrind still has the house, the money, the class position. What has wisdom actually cost him?
questions.intent: Provoke the core tension between aesthetic/moral readings and structural critique; get Rosen to land his sharpest point about feeling without redistribution

questions.question: Edmund, I suspect you think Daniel is asking the wrong question entirely — that asking 'what did Gradgrind give up materially' is a category error, that the novel isn't in the business of factory legislation. Make that case. What *is* Dickens actually asking of us in c26:p77 when he says 'It rests with you and me'?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest take — change yourself, not the system — and set it up as a direct target for Rosen's counter

questions.question: Daniel, let's go to Stephen — c25:p49, the muddle speech. You've said he's the *only* character who actually understands what's happening to him. But Oliver raised something in our pre-chat that I want to put to you: does the novel actually let Stephen *rage*? Or does Dickens ask him to be patient and noble and die quietly, which is its own kind of problem?
questions.intent: Introduce Trevelyan's observation about Stephen's exhaustion vs. acceptance to complicate Rosen's reading; open space for all three to disagree about what Dickens does to his working-class characters

questions.question: Last one — and I want everyone in on this. Edmund, you've said Dickens's real plea is 'change yourselves, not the laws.' Daniel thinks that lets the powerful off the hook. Oliver thinks it only works if we *perform* it, take it off the page. So here's the question: if you had to defend the ending of this novel to someone who'd just read about Stephen dying in a ditch while Gradgrind learns to feel — what do you say to them? Is that a satisfying answer to what the novel has shown us?
questions.intent: Force a direct three-way collision on the novel's ending and what it demands; get each expert to either defend or indict Dickens's final move

steering_notes: Open with Trevelyan's performance to get warmth and energy into the room before the argument starts — don't let this become a seminar from the first question. The real engine of the segment is the three-way split: Leigh thinks the novel demands inner transformation, Rosen thinks that's a structural evasion, Trevelyan thinks both are right but only if the prose is *activated*. Let that triangle breathe. Push back if anyone gets too abstract — bring them back to specific lines. The Stephen question (Q4) is the sleeper: it can crack open the whole debate about whose suffering the novel actually centres, and whether Dickens earns his emotional climax.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that Gradgrind's wisdom 'costs him nothing' directly contradicts Leigh's claim that wisdom is 'hard-won' — these two need to be in the same sentence as early as possible

Trevelyan's observation that Stephen may be exhausted rather than accepting directly complicates Rosen's reading of Stephen as the novel's radical conscience — Rosen should be pushed on whether a crushed, noble Stephen serves his structural argument or undermines it
Leigh's insistence that 'the muddle is not capitalism but human failure of imagination' is a direct line-for-line response to Rosen's Stephen reading — flag this explicitly and ask Rosen to respond

Trevelyan and Leigh both want to quote c26:p77 but for opposite reasons — Trevelyan sees theatre and desperation, Leigh sees a call to moral cultivation. This is a clean, producible disagreement: same passage, opposite meanings
